draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

lines: -I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

+I watched boardings rise from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. That jump feels like success until I look for context. I need to know how many people were actually present to use the service. Without that denominator, the raw counts only show trips taken, not how the option was received across the whole student body. The numbers themselves are clear, but their meaning stays hidden until I can connect those trips to the broader population’s actual access.

-My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+The missing attendance figures prevent me from distinguishing a rise in ridership from a simple increase in campus population or class participation. No attendance data were collected during the pilot [@lyra:1]. Consequently, I cannot tell whether more students chose the shuttle or whether more students were present to use it. This quantitative gap limits the interpretation of the boarding counts before I even address the survey’s representativeness issues.

+The survey data presents a parallel limitation. Only voluntary riders participated, while non-riders were excluded entirely [@lyra:2]. Without input from those who did not use the service, I cannot determine whether their avoidance stems from preference, accessibility barriers, or schedule conflicts. Consequently, the rider responses reflect a self-selected group rather than the broader student population. This omission means the qualitative evidence, like the quantitative counts, fails to capture the full scope of campus transportation needs.

+Given these gaps, I propose extending the pilot for one term, contingent on resolving the non-rider data deficit. The boarding counts, ranging from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1], suggest usage but do not confirm broader demand, particularly since no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], I cannot yet assess whether barriers prevent participation. Therefore, the extension should be conditional on successfully measuring access for those who currently avoid the service, ensuring the next evaluation captures actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.

+Since the initial study excluded non-riders [@lyra:2], I propose surveying them directly to identify specific barriers preventing use. To reach this population effectively, a digital link sent to the general student body offers the most inclusive and low-cost channel. This method targets the identified data gap without inventing new operational costs or requiring additional staff. Collecting this feedback during the one-term extension will determine whether existing barriers are structural or informational, ensuring the evaluation reflects actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.

## Evidence

I watched boardings rise from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. That jump feels like success until I look for context. I need to know how many people were actually present to use the service. Without that denominator, the raw counts only show trips taken, not how the option was received across the whole student body. The numbers themselves are clear, but their meaning stays hidden until I can connect those trips to the broader population’s actual access.

The missing attendance figures prevent me from distinguishing a rise in ridership from a simple increase in campus population or class participation. No attendance data were collected during the pilot [@lyra:1]. Consequently, I cannot tell whether more students chose the shuttle or whether more students were present to use it. This quantitative gap limits the interpretation of the boarding counts before I even address the survey’s representativeness issues.

The survey data presents a parallel limitation. Only voluntary riders participated, while non-riders were excluded entirely [@lyra:2]. Without input from those who did not use the service, I cannot determine whether their avoidance stems from preference, accessibility barriers, or schedule conflicts. Consequently, the rider responses reflect a self-selected group rather than the broader student population. This omission means the qualitative evidence, like the quantitative counts, fails to capture the full scope of campus transportation needs.

## Recommendation

Given these gaps, I propose extending the pilot for one term, contingent on resolving the non-rider data deficit. The boarding counts, ranging from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1], suggest usage but do not confirm broader demand, particularly since no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], I cannot yet assess whether barriers prevent participation. Therefore, the extension should be conditional on successfully measuring access for those who currently avoid the service, ensuring the next evaluation captures actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.

Since the initial study excluded non-riders [@lyra:2], I propose surveying them directly to identify specific barriers preventing use. To reach this population effectively, a digital link sent to the general student body offers the most inclusive and low-cost channel. This method targets the identified data gap without inventing new operational costs or requiring additional staff. Collecting this feedback during the one-term extension will determine whether existing barriers are structural or informational, ensuring the evaluation reflects actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.

blocks.content: Given these gaps, I propose extending the pilot for one term, contingent on resolving the non-rider data deficit. The boarding counts, ranging from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1], suggest usage but do not confirm broader demand, particularly since no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. live_draft_suggestions.base_content:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: I watched boardings rise from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. That jump feels like success until I look for context. I need to know how many people were actually present to use the service. Without that denominator, the raw counts only show trips taken, not how the option was received across the whole student body. The numbers themselves are clear, but their meaning stays hidden until I can connect those trips to the broader population’s actual access.

live_draft_blocks.content: Given these gaps, I propose extending the pilot for one term, contingent on resolving the non-rider data deficit. The boarding counts, ranging from 160 in week A to 240 in week B [@lyra:1], suggest usage but do not confirm broader demand, particularly since no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], I cannot yet assess whether barriers prevent participation. Therefore, the extension should be conditional on successfully measuring access for those who currently avoid the service, ensuring the next evaluation captures actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Since the initial study excluded non-riders [@lyra:2], I propose surveying them directly to identify specific barriers preventing use. To reach this population effectively, a digital link sent to the general student body offers the most inclusive and low-cost channel. This method targets the identified data gap without inventing new operational costs or requiring additional staff. Collecting this feedback during the one-term extension will determine whether existing barriers are structural or informational, ensuring the evaluation reflects actual usage constraints rather than just voluntary rider experiences.
